options: An identifier that sits at the same grain as the fact row but has no descriptive attributes, so it's kept on the fact table instead of a separate dimension table
A dimension table that has been deleted from the warehouse by mistake
A dimension table with more than a million rows
A fact table that has no measure columns
questions.explain: The classic example is a sales order number — it's an identifier at the fact table's own grain, with no attributes of its own to justify a separate table.

questions.q: Why doesn't a sales order number get its own dimension table?
options: It has no descriptive attributes to filter or group by, so a separate table would only add a join with no benefit
SQL Server doesn't allow single-column dimension tables
Order numbers are always duplicated across multiple sales facts
It would violate the star schema's naming convention
questions.explain: A dimension table earns its place by offering attributes to filter and group by; an order number alone offers nothing the fact table doesn't already have.

questions.q: How can you present a degenerate dimension to report authors as if it were a real dimension table?
options: Wrap it in a view that selects the distinct identifier column from the fact table
Copy the column into every other dimension table in the warehouse
It's impossible — degenerate dimensions can never be queried like a dimension
Convert the fact table's primary key into a foreign key
questions.explain: A CREATE VIEW statement selecting DISTINCT values from the fact table's identifier column gives downstream tools something that looks like a dimension table, without storing a redundant copy.

questions.q: Which of these is a realistic real-world example of a degenerate dimension?
options: An invoice number or ticket number kept directly on a fact table
A product's color and category, stored on DimProduct
A customer's full mailing address, stored on DimCustomer
A calendar year, stored on DimDate
questions.explain: Invoice numbers, ticket numbers, and order numbers are classic degenerate dimensions — identifiers with no attributes of their own, at the fact table's own grain.

questions.q: What two questions determine whether an identifier is a degenerate dimension candidate?
options: Does it sit at the same grain as the fact row, and does it carry zero descriptive attributes of its own?
Is it an integer, and is it under 10 characters long?
Was it created before the fact table, and is it indexed?
Does it appear in more than one fact table, and is it a foreign key?
questions.explain: If an identifier matches the fact table's grain exactly and has no attributes worth storing separately, it's a degenerate dimension — leave it on the fact table.
